The core insight is that language functions as a dynamic communication network where meaning emerges from interaction rather than fixed grammar. The transition from Classical Latin to modern usage reflects a bifurcation in communicative purpose—academic vs. practical. This duality creates a failure mode where specialized knowledge becomes isolated from broader societal needs. The linguistic communication network primitive formalizes this as a stochastic system with entropy-driven evolution. The classical Latin isolation primitive captures the stratification effect, where increasing specialization leads to semantic dead ends. Modern language adaptation highlights the necessity of linguistic flexibility for cognitive integration. These primitives converge on a universal lens: language as a self-organizing system governed by information-theoretic principles.
